meta.title: Vercel SDR — example outbound messages
meta.description: First-touch email drafts from the demo pipeline mock data. These illustrate angle types (hiring signal, social post, event, tech migration, trial activation) and tone patterns the app reviews before send.

examples.tactic: Pair public hiring language with internal trial/preview activation so the opener feels timely, not generic.
examples.subject: Scaling preview workflow as Acme ramps up
examples.body:
Hi Sarah,

Saw Acme is hiring around frontend platform workflow just as your Vercel workspace activity picked up this week.

That usually means preview environments and release coordination are becoming more important fast. We have been helping engineering teams tighten that part of the rollout without adding more internal process. Open to a quick compare-notes conversation?

Best,
examples.highlightedSpan: That usually means preview environments and release coordination are becoming more important fast.

examples.tactic: Lead with the prospect’s own narrative (reducing sprawl) and support with docs-intent signals without sounding surveillance-heavy.
examples.subject: Platform consolidation timing at LedgerLoop
examples.body:
Hi Devin,

Your note about reducing platform sprawl stood out, especially since LedgerLoop has been back in the weeds on routing and middleware questions this week.

We work with platform teams when that consolidation effort starts turning into release-workflow decisions. If that is on your plate this quarter, open to a quick comparison call?

Best,
examples.highlightedSpan: We work with platform teams when that consolidation effort starts turning into release-workflow decisions.

examples.tactic: Anchor on a public event (webinar) for regulated context; keep internal page visits as supporting evidence only.
examples.subject: Secure release workflow for regulated teams
examples.body:
Hi Alana,

Saw Northstar joined the healthcare infrastructure webinar on secure release workflow. That topic tends to come up when teams want tighter control without slowing engineers down.

We have been helping regulated engineering orgs simplify preview access, auditability, and release guardrails. Would a short conversation be useful?

Best,
examples.highlightedSpan: That topic tends to come up when teams want tighter control without slowing engineers down.

examples.tactic: Tie public engineering content (release workflow) to recurring product usage so the pitch stays operational.
examples.subject: Simplifying release workflow at BrightOps

Best,

examples.subject: Product @ Eragon – a16z Seed – Applied AI for Enterprise – SF

Hi Brandon,

I’m working with Josh Sirota [https://www.linkedin.com/in/josh-sirota/], founder of Eragon [https://www.eragon.ai/], an Applied AI Lab for the Enterprise. 

They raised a large Seed from a16z, SOMA, & Long Journey (Zuck's sister) and are hiring the Founding Engineering team.

Problem Space [https://eragon-ai.notion.site/Exciting-Problems-We-Are-Working-On-2af25c3be529807896c8faa0e99eb341]

Eragon is betting the next wave of AI won’t come from bigger foundation models, but from smaller, proprietary models trained directly on a company’s own data to power an internal AI workforce.

They’re building the full stack to make that possible. Training infra, agent frameworks, orchestration, and developer tooling so enterprises can run secure, reasoning-capable agents inside their most complex ops teams. 

Why this is a standout opportunity
* Own the stack for enterprise AI workforces — not wrappers around OpenAI, but custom-trained small models and agent systems that companies rely on daily
* Real infra problems — inference, orchestration, observability, retrieval, tool use, latency at scale
* Model + infra + agents in one place — training pipelines, agent frameworks, and developer tools under one roof
* Top of market comp — $250K–$500K base + 1–5% equity for early team ownership
* Founding team from DeepMind, FAIR, Salesforce, Waterloo + $1M+ in GPU grants

If interested, I’d love to connect!

Chad Rogers 
Partner @ Quantum | Ex-Grammarly, Stripe, and Meta.

Hey Brandon, quick nudge in case this got buried.

Not sure if you were at NRF this year, but I found a lot of the perspectives around how large retailers are actually using agentic AI in production pretty interesting. There was a noticeable shift away from “what’s possible” toward “what’s actually holding up at scale,” which sounds aligned with a lot of what you write about.

I’ve worked with product teams where images quietly become part of the ops surface area faster than expected. Not as a creative problem, but as another input the system has to trust, standardize, and move through reliably. It often ends up sitting just outside the core platform until it suddenly becomes a bottleneck.

No pitch here, mostly curious how you’re thinking about this at Wonder, or whether it’s already something your team has strong opinions on. Happy to compare notes if it’s useful.

– D’Angelo

Hi Brandon,

I came across your profile and your work around agentic AI and production-grade systems really stood out. Given how focused you are on making AI safe, auditable, and actually usable in real workflows, I thought it was worth reaching out.

At Photoroom, we apply GenAI in a very operational way. Large food and delivery platforms like DoorDash use us as a core production workflow to automate and govern image processing at scale, especially around product and menu imagery that flows across multiple systems.

What tends to resonate with teams like yours is how we treat imagery as structured data, not just creative output — with deterministic rules, quality controls, and automation that can plug cleanly into existing platforms rather than live as a one-off tool.

I’d love to show you how we’re approaching this from an AI and systems perspective and get your take on whether it maps to how Wonder is thinking about agentic workflows today. Happy to keep it lightweight.

Best,
D’Angelo
